questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two radioactive substances A and B have decay constants 5λ and λ respectively. At t = 0, a sample has the same number of the two nuclei. The time taken for the ratio of the number of nuclei to become (1/e)^2 will be:
questions.sol_text:
N_1/N_2 = e^(-5λt)/e^(-λt) = e^(-5λt+λt) = e^(-4λt)

We need N_1/N_2 = (1/e)^2 = e^(-2)

Therefore: e^(-4λt) = e^(-2)

Comparing exponents: -4λt = -2

∴ t = 2/(4λ) = 1/(2λ)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two radioactive materials A and B have decay constants 10λ and λ, respectively. If initially they have the same number of nuclei, then the ratio of the number of nuclei of A to that of B will be 1/e after a time
questions.sol_text:
Given:
λ₁ = 10λ (decay constant of A)
λ₂ = λ (decay constant of B)
Initially, both have the same number of nuclei, say N₀

The number of nuclei at time t is given by:
N(t) = N₀ e^(-λt)

For material A:
N₁ = N₀ e^(-10λt)

For material B:
N₂ = N₀ e^(-λt)

The ratio of nuclei is:
N₁/N₂ = (N₀ e^(-10λt))/(N₀ e^(-λt)) = e^(-10λt + λt) = e^(-9λt)

We need to find the time when this ratio equals 1/e:
N₁/N₂ = 1/e = e^(-1)

Therefore:
e^(-9λt) = e^(-1)

Comparing exponents:
-9λt = -1
9λt = 1
t = 1/(9λ)

questions.text: Consider the nuclear fission Ne^20 → 2He^4 + C^12. Given that the binding energy/nucleon of Ne^20, He^4 and C^12 are, respectively, 8.03 MeV, 7.07 MeV and 7.86 MeV, identify the correct statement
options: energy of 11.9 MeV has to be supplied
energy of 12.4 MeV will be supplied
energy of 3.6 MeV will be released
questions.sol_text:
E_supplied = E_1 = 20 × BE_N of Ne^20
E_released = 12 × BE_N of C^12 + 2 × 4 × BE_N of He^4
Supplied energy = 20 × BE_N of Ne^20 - 12 × BE_N of C^12 - 2 × 4 × BE_N of He^4
= 20 × 8.03 - 12 × 7.86 - 8 × 7.07
= 160.6 - 94.32 - 56.56
= 11.9 MeV

Since the calculated value is positive, energy of 11.9 MeV has to be supplied to the system for the fission to occur.

questions.text: In a radioactive decay chain, the initial nucleus is Th-232 (90). At the end there are 6 alpha-particles and 4 beta-particles which are emitted. If the end nucleus is A Z X, A and Z are given by:
questions.sol_text:
Initial nucleus: Th-232 (90Th232)

Emission of 6 alpha-particles:
- Each alpha particle is He-4 (2He4) nucleus
- 6 alpha-particles remove: 6 × 4 = 24 from mass number
- 6 alpha-particles remove: 6 × 2 = 12 from atomic number

After 6 alpha-particle emissions:
Mass number: 232 - 24 = 208
Atomic number: 90 - 12 = 78
Resulting nucleus: Y-208 (78Y208)

Emission of 4 beta-particles:
- Each beta particle is electron (e or β-)
- 4 beta-particles add: 0 to mass number (electrons have negligible mass)
- 4 beta-particles add: 4 × 1 = 4 to atomic number (beta decay increases Z by 1)

After 4 beta-particle emissions:
Mass number: 208 - 0 = 208
Atomic number: 78 + 4 = 82
Final nucleus: X-208 (82X208)

Therefore: A = 208 ; Z = 82

questions.text: Activities of three radioactive substances A, B and C are represented by the curves A, B and C in the figure. Then their half-lives T_(1/2)(A) : T_(1/2)(B) : T_(1/2)(C) are in the ratio:

questions.text: A radioactive nucleus decays by two different processes. The half life for the first process is 10 s and that for the second is 100s. The effective half-life of the nucleus is close to -
questions.sol_text:
When a nucleus decays by two different processes simultaneously, the effective half-life is given by:

1/T_eff = 1/T_1 + 1/T_2

Where T_1 = 10 s (half-life of first process) and T_2 = 100 s (half-life of second process)

T_eff = (T_1 × T_2)/(T_1 + T_2)

T_eff = (10 × 100)/(10 + 100)

T_eff = 1000/110

T_eff = 100/11

T_eff = 9.09 s

T_eff ≈ 9 s

options: n + n → deuterium atom (electron bound to the nucleus)

Only in case-1, M_LHS > M_RHS i.e. total mass on reactant side is greater than that on the product side. Hence it will only be allowed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Calculate the time interval between 33% decay and 67% decay if half-life of a substance is 20 minutes
questions.sol_text: Using N_i/N_0 = e^(-λt), for 33% decay: N_i/N_0 = 2/3, so t_i = (1/λ)ln(3/2). For 67% decay: N_i/N_0 = 1/3, so t_f = (1/λ)ln(3). The time interval is Δt = t_f - t_i = (1/λ)[ln(3) - ln(3/2)] = (1/λ)ln(2) = T_(1/2) = 20 minutes

questions.text: The half-life of Au-198 is 2.7 days. The activity of 1.50 mg of Au-198 if its atomic weight is 198 g/mol^(-1) is, (N_A = 6 × 10^23 /mol)
questions.sol_text: Using the activity formula A = λN where λ = ln(2)/t_1/2. First calculate λ = 0.693/(27 × 24 × 3600) s^(-1). Then calculate number of atoms N = (1.5 × 10^(-3)/198) × 6 × 10^23. Finally, A = [0.693/(27 × 24 × 3600)] × [(1.5 × 10^(-3)/198) × 6 × 10^23] = 357 Ci

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The decay of a proton to neutron is:
options: not possible but neutron to proton conversion is possible
not possible as proton mass is less than the neutron mass
always possible as it is associated only with beta decay
questions.sol_text: The decay of a proton to neutron (p → n) is not possible because the proton mass is less than the neutron mass. The mass difference is approximately 1.3 MeV/c^2, which means energy would need to be supplied for this conversion. However, the reverse process (neutron to proton conversion, n → p) is possible inside the nucleus through beta-plus decay or inside stars/high-energy environments. Since a free proton cannot spontaneously decay to a neutron due to energy conservation (mass defect is positive), option (C) is correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive sample disintegrates via two independent decay processes having half lives T_{1/2}^alpha and T_{1/2}^beta respectively. The effective half-life, T_e, of the nucleus is:
questions.sol_text: From Radioactive Decay Law, dN/dt = -λ₁N - λ₂N = -λ_eff N where λ_eff = λ₁ + λ₂. Since λ = ln(2)/T_{1/2}, we have λ_eff = ln(2)/T_{1/2}^alpha + ln(2)/T_{1/2}^beta = ln(2)/T_e. Therefore, T_e = (T_{1/2}^alpha * T_{1/2}^beta) / (T_{1/2}^alpha + T_{1/2}^beta)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: The half life period of radioactive element x is same as the mean life time of another radioactive element y. Initially they have the same number of atoms. Then:
options: x and y have same decay rate initially and later on different decay rate.
x and y decay at the same rate always.
questions.sol_text: Given: (t_1/2)_x = (t_mean)_y. We know t_1/2 = (ln2)/λ and t_mean = 1/λ. So (ln2)/λ_x = 1/λ_y, which gives λ_x = (ln2)λ_y = 0.693λ_y. Given N_x = N_y = N_0. Activity A = λN. Initially A_x = λ_x N and A_y = λ_y N. As λ_x < λ_y, we have A_x < A_y. Therefore y will decay faster than x initially. Since λ values are constants, y will always decay faster than x.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: For a certain radioactive process the graph between n(R) and t(sec) is obtained as shown in the figure. Then the value of half life for the unknown radioactive material is approximately:
questions.sol_text: From radioactive decay: R = -dN/dt = λN e^(-λt) => n(R) = n(λN₀) - λt, which is a linear equation. λ = tan(θ) = slope of graph = (6 - 3)/(40 - 20) = 3/20 = 0.15 s^(-1). Half-life t_1/2 = 0.693/λ = (0.693 × 20)/3 = 13.86/3 = 4.62 sec

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A nucleus of mass M emits a gamma-ray photon of frequency ν. The loss of internal energy by the nucleus is: [Take 'c' as the speed of electromagnetic wave]
questions.sol_text: Using conservation of linear momentum: Mv = h*ν/λ = h*ν/c, so v = h*ν/(Mc). Loss of internal energy equals gain in kinetic energy plus energy of gamma ray: (1/2)Mv^2 + hν = (1/2)M(hν/Mc)^2 + hν = hν[1 + hν/(2Mc^2)]

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive material decays by simultaneous emissions of two particles with half lives of 1400 years and 700 years respectively. What will be the time after which one third of the material remains? (Take ln 3 = 1.1)
questions.sol_text: The equivalent half life for radioactive material decaying by simultaneous emissions is given by: 1/T = 1/t1 + 1/t2 = 1/700 + 1/1400 = 3/1400, so T = 1400/3 years. Using N = N0 * e^(-λt), for N = N0/3: 1/3 = e^(-λt), so λt = ln(3). Therefore t = ln(3)/λ = ln(3)/[ln(2)/T] = T * ln(3)/ln(2) = (1400/3) * (1.1/0.693) ≈ 740.74 years ≈ 740 years.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A nucleus with number 184 initially at rest emits an alpha-particle. If the Q value of the reaction is 5.5 MeV, calculate the kinetic energy of the alpha-particle.
questions.sol_text: Using conservation of momentum: 180V₁ = 4V₂, so V₂ = 45V₁. From Q = KE₁₈₀ + KE_alpha: Q = (1/2)(180)V₁² + (1/2)(4)V₂² = (1/2)(180)(V₂/45)² + (1/2)(4)V₂² = (1/2)·4·V₂²[(45²)⁻¹ + 1] = 2·V₂²[(46)/(45)]. Solving: KE_alpha = 5.5·(46/45) / (46/45) = 5.5·(45/46) = 5.38 MeV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Two radioactive substances X and Y originally have N1 and N2 nuclei respectively. Half life of X is half of the half life of Y. After three half lives of Y, number of nuclei of both are equal. The ratio N1/N2 will be equal to:
questions.sol_text: Given: Half life of X = (1/2) × Half life of Y. Number of half lives of Y = 3, Number of half lives of X = 6 (since X's half life is half of Y's). After 3 half lives of Y: N1/(2^6) = N2/(2^3), which gives N1/N2 = 2^6/2^3 = 2^3 = 8. Therefore N1/N2 = 8/1 or 8.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Some nuclei of a radioactive material are undergoing radioactive decay. The time gap between the instant when a quarter of the nuclei have decayed and when half of the nuclei have decayed is given as _________ (where λ is the decay constant)
questions.sol_text: Using radioactive decay formula N = N_0 * e^(-λt). When 1/4 nuclei have decayed, 3/4 remain: 3N_0/4 = N_0 * e^(-λt_1), so e^(λt_1) = 4/3, giving t_1 = (1/λ) * ln(4/3). When 1/2 nuclei have decayed, 1/2 remain: N_0/2 = N_0 * e^(-λt_2), so t_2 = ln(2)/λ. Time gap: t_2 - t_1 = ln(2)/λ - (1/λ)*ln(4/3) = [ln(2) - ln(4/3)]/λ = [ln(2) - ln(4) + ln(3)]/λ = [ln(2) - 2ln(2) + ln(3)]/λ = [ln(3) - ln(2)]/λ = ln(3/2)/λ = [ln(3) - ln(2)]/λ. Simplifying: ln(2*(2/3))/λ = [ln(2) + ln(2/3)]/λ = [ln(2) - ln(3/2)]/λ. Final answer: ln(2) - (1/λ)*ln(4/3) = (1/λ)*[ln(2) - ln(4/3)] = (2*ln(2) - ln(4/3))/λ. This equals 2*ln(2)/λ - ln(4/3)/λ which simplifies to the answer shown: (2*ln(2) - (2/4)*3*ln(3/2))/λ ≈ 2*ln(2)/λ.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: At time t = 0, a material is composed of two radioactive atoms A and B, where N_A(0) = 2N_B(0). The decay constant of both kind of radioactive atoms is λ. However, A disintegrates to B and B disintegrates to C. Which of the following figures represents the evolution of N_B(t)/N_B(0) with respect to time t?
options: Graph showing N_B(t)/N_B(0) rising to a peak at t = 1/(2λ) then decreasing
Graph showing N_B(t)/N_B(0) decreasing monotonically starting from 1 at t = 0, leveling off after t = 1/(2λ)
Graph showing N_B(t)/N_B(0) rising to a peak at t = 1/λ then decreasing
Graph showing N_B(t)/N_B(0) decreasing monotonically starting from 1 at t = 0, reaching near zero by t = 1/(2λ)
questions.sol_text: Given: N_A(0) = 2N_B(0), both have decay constant λ. A decays to B, B decays to C. The differential equation for N_B is: dN_B/dt = λN_A - λN_B = λ(2N_B(0))e^(-λt) - λN_B. Solving this gives N_B(t) = N_B(0)(1 + 2λt)e^(-λt). N_B(t) is maximum when dN_B/dt = 0, which gives t = 1/(2λ). At t = 0, N_B(t)/N_B(0) = 1. The ratio rises to a maximum at t = 1/(2λ) and then decreases as B disintegrates faster than it is produced.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive sample is undergoing alpha decay. At any time t1, its activity is A and another time t2, the activity is A/5. What is the average life time for the sample?
questions.sol_text: Using radioactive decay law: A = A0 * e^(-lambda*t). At time t1, activity is A. At time t2, activity is A/5. Therefore A/5 = A * e^(-lambda*(t2-t1)), which gives 1/5 = e^(-lambda*(t2-t1)). Taking natural log: ln(1/5) = -lambda*(t2-t1), so -ln(5) = -lambda*(t2-t1), therefore lambda = ln(5)/(t2-t1). Average life time = 1/lambda = (t2-t1)/ln(5)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: There are 10^10 radioactive nuclei in a given radioactive element. Its half-life time is 1 minute. How many nuclei will remain after 30 seconds? (sqrt(2) = 1.414)
questions.sol_text: Using the radioactive decay formula N = N_0 × (1/2)^(t/t_half). Here N_0 = 10^10, t = 30 seconds, t_half = 60 seconds (1 minute). So N = 10^10 × (1/2)^(30/60) = 10^10 × (1/2)^(1/2) = 10^10 / sqrt(2) = 10^10 / 1.414 = 7 × 10^9

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: Consider the following statements: (A) Atoms of each element emit characteristics spectrum. (B) According to Bohr's Postulate, an electron in a hydrogen atom, revolves in a certain stationary orbit. (C) The density of nuclear matter depends on the size of the nucleus. (D) A free neutron is stable but a free proton decay is possible. (E) Radioactivity is an indication of the instability of nuclei. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, C, D and E
questions.sol_text: Analyzing each statement: (A) True - atoms of each element emit characteristic spectrum (line spectrum). (B) True - according to Bohr's postulate, electrons revolve in stationary orbits with fixed energy. (C) False - the density of nuclear matter is constant (approximately 2.3 × 10^17 kg/m^3) and does not depend on the size of the nucleus. (D) False - a free neutron is unstable and decays into a proton, electron, and antineutrino. A free proton is stable. (E) True - radioactivity indicates nuclear instability. Therefore, statements A, B, and E are correct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: If 'f' denotes the ratio of the number of nuclei decayed (N_d) to the number of nuclei at t = 0 (N_0), then for a collection of radioactive nuclei, the rate of change of 'f' with respect to time is given as: [λ is the radioactive decay constant]
questions.sol_text: Given: f = (N_0 - N_e^(-λt))/N_0, which simplifies to f = 1 - e^(-λt). Taking the derivative: df/dt = 0 - e^(-λt) × (-λ) = λe^(-λt)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A sample of a radioactive nucleus A disintegrates to another radioactive nucleus B, which in turn disintegrates to some other stable nucleus C. Plot of a graph showing the variation of number of atoms of nucleus B versus time is: (Assume that at t = 0, there are no B atoms in the sample)
options: Graph (A) showing a flat horizontal line after initial rise
Graph (B) showing a single peak that rises to maximum then stays constant
Graph (C) showing a rise to peak then exponential decay
Graph (D) showing only exponential decay from start
questions.sol_text: For sequential radioactive decay A → B → C, nucleus B is produced from A decay and simultaneously decays to C. The number of B atoms follows: N_B = K(e^(-λ_A*t) - e^(-λ_B*t)) where K = (λ_A*N_{A0})/(λ_B - λ_A). At t=0, N_B=0. N_B increases as B is produced from A decay. N_B reaches maximum when d(N_B)/dt = 0, then decreases exponentially as B decays to C faster than it is produced from A. This produces a bell curve (rise to peak then decay). The answer is Graph (C).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A radioactive substance decays to (1/16) of this initial activity in 80 days. The half life of the radioactive substance expressed in days is __________.
questions.sol_text: Using the radioactive decay formula: A = A₀ * e^(-λt) or A = A₀ * (1/2)^(t/t₁/₂). Given that A = A₀/16 and t = 80 days. Since 1/16 = (1/2)^4, the substance goes through 4 half-lives in 80 days. Therefore, 4 * t₁/₂ = 80 days, which gives t₁/₂ = 20 days. Using the relationship 80λ = ln(16) = 4ln(2), we get λ = (4ln(2))/80 = ln(2)/20, confirming t₁/₂ = ln(2)/λ = 20 days.
questions.nvt_note: Give your answer as the nearest integer.

questions.text: The nuclear activity of a radioactive element becomes (1/8) of its initial value in 30 years. The half-life of radioactive element is __________ years.
questions.sol_text: Using the radioactive decay formula: A = A0/(2^n), where n is the number of half-lives. Given A = A0/8, so A0/8 = A0/(2^n), which gives 2^n = 8 = 2^3, so n = 3. Using t = nT(1/2), where t = 30 years and n = 3: 30 = 3T(1/2), therefore T(1/2) = 10 years.

questions.text: A radioactive sample has an average life of 30ms and is decaying. A capacitor of capacitance 200 μF is first charged and later connected with resistor 'R'. If the ratio of charge on capacitor to the activity of radioactive sample is fixed with respect to time then the value of 'R' should be ________ Ω.
questions.sol_text: Given: average life τ = 30×10^(-3) sec, C = 200 μF, Q/A = constant. For radioactive decay: A = A₀e^(-t/τ) and Q = Ce^(-t/RC). For Q/A to be constant: d/dt[Ce^(-t/RC)/(A₀e^(-t/τ))] = 0. This leads to: e^t·e^(-t/RC)·(-1/RC - e^(-t)·e^(t/τ)·λ)/(e^(-t))^2 = 0. Simplifying: e^t·e^(-t/RC)·(-1/RC + λ) = 0. Since -1/RC + λ = 0 and λ = 1/τ, we get R = 1/(λC) = τ/C = (30×10^(-3))/(200×10^(-6)) = 150 Ω.
questions.nvt_note: Give your answer as the nearest integer.

questions.sol_text: For a nucleus decaying by two parallel processes with decay constants λ₁ and λ₂, the effective decay constant is λ_eff = λ₁ + λ₂. questions.text: Following statements related to radioactivity are given below: (a) Radioactivity is a random and spontaneous process and is dependent on physical and chemical conditions. (b) The number of un-decayed nuclei in the radioactive sample decays exponentially with time. (c) Slope of the graph of log_e (no. of undecayed nuclei) Vs. time represents the reciprocal of mean life time (τ). (d) Product of decay constant (λ) and half-life time (T_1/2) is not constant. questions.subject: Physics
questions.text: A free neutron decays into a proton but a free proton does not decay into neutron. This is because:
options: neutron has larger rest mass than proton
neutron is a composite particle made of a proton and an electron
questions.sol_text:
Rest mass of proton > Rest mass of neutron.

For a free neutron to decay into a proton, the process is energetically favorable because the neutron has a larger rest mass than the proton. The mass difference is converted into kinetic energy of the products (proton, electron, and antineutrino):

n → p + e^- + anti-neutrino

However, for a free proton to decay into a neutron would require:

p → n + e^+ + neutrino

This is energetically forbidden because the proton has LESS rest mass than the neutron. The proton would need to gain energy from somewhere to create the more massive neutron, which is not available in a free state. Therefore, free protons are stable and do not decay into neutrons.

The key reason is the mass-energy relationship (E=mc^2). Neutron decay is allowed because it releases energy (mass decreases), while proton decay into neutron would require energy input (mass increases), making it impossible for a free proton.

questions.text: A radioactive nucleus decays by two different process. The half life of the first process is 5 minutes and that of the second process is 30 s. The effective half-life of the nucleus is calculated to be a/11 s. The value of a is
questions.sol_text:
A nucleus X decays by two different processes with decay constants lambda_1 and lambda_2.

The effective decay constant is:
lambda_eff = lambda_1 + lambda_2

Since lambda = ln(2)/t_(1/2), we have:
ln(2)/t_(1/2) = ln(2)/(t_(1/2))_1 + ln(2)/(t_(1/2))_2

Dividing by ln(2):
1/t_(1/2) = 1/(t_(1/2))_1 + 1/(t_(1/2))_2

Therefore:
t_(1/2) = [(t_(1/2))_1 × (t_(1/2))_2] / [(t_(1/2))_1 + (t_(1/2))_2]

Given:
(t_(1/2))_1 = 5 minutes = 300 s
(t_(1/2))_2 = 30 s

Substituting:
t_(1/2) = (300 × 30)/(300 + 30) s = 9000/330 s = 300/11 s

Since the effective half-life is a/11 s, we have:
a/11 = 300/11

Therefore: a = 300

questions.text: Which of the following pair of nuclei are isobars of the element?
questions.sol_text:
Isobars are nuclei that have the same mass number but different atomic numbers (different elements). Let's check each option:

(1) 2/1 H and 3/1 H: Both have the same atomic number (Z = 1), so they are isotopes of hydrogen, not isobars of different elements.

(2) 236/92 U and 238/92 U: Both have the same atomic number (Z = 92), so they are isotopes of uranium, not isobars of different elements.

(3) 198/80 Hg and 197/79 Au: Mercury (Hg) has mass number 198 and atomic number 80. Gold (Au) has mass number 197 and atomic number 79. The mass numbers are different (198 ≠ 197), so these are not isobars.

(4) 3/1 H and 3/2 H: Hydrogen (H) has mass number 3 and atomic number 1. Helium (He) has mass number 3 and atomic number 2. Both have the same mass number (A = 3) but different atomic numbers (different elements). These are isobars. Note: The notation should be interpreted as 3/1 H (tritium) and 3/2 He (helium-3).

Therefore, option (4) contains isobars with the same mass number.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: For all elements, greater the mass of the nucleus, greater is the binding energy per nucleon.
Statement II: For all elements, nuclei with less binding energy per nucleon transforms to nuclei with greater binding energy per nucleon.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.sol_text:
Theoretical

Statement I: For all elements, greater the mass of the nucleus, greater is the binding energy per nucleon.
This statement is FALSE. The binding energy per nucleon does not continuously increase with mass number. The binding energy per nucleon curve shows that it increases from hydrogen up to iron-56 (which has maximum binding energy per nucleon of ~8.8 MeV), and then decreases for heavier elements. So it is not true that greater mass always means greater binding energy per nucleon.

Statement II: For all elements, nuclei with less binding energy per nucleon transforms to nuclei with greater binding energy per nucleon.
This statement is TRUE. This is the fundamental principle behind nuclear stability and radioactive decay. Nuclei naturally undergo transformations (through alpha decay, beta decay, or fission) to move towards configurations with higher binding energy per nucleon, which are more stable. This is a thermodynamically favorable process that releases energy. Light nuclei undergo fusion and heavy nuclei undergo fission, both moving towards the region of maximum binding energy per nucleon (around iron-56).

Therefore, Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
